# Paul Irving

## Overview

- **Age:** 16 years old  <sub>[v3 c40 P2](../source/v03-c40.md#nw-v03-c40-p0002)</sub>
- **Gender:** male  <sub>[v2 c5 P8](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0008)</sub>
- **Origin:** Boston, the States  <sub>[v2 c1 P45](../source/v02-c01.md#nw-v02-c01-p0045), [v2 c11 P38](../source/v02-c11.md#nw-v02-c11-p0038), [v2 c21 P83](../source/v02-c21.md#nw-v02-c21-p0083)</sub>
- **Role:** Poet and student  <sub>[v4 c3 P33](../source/v04-c03.md#nw-v04-c03-p0033), [v4 c17 P27](../source/v04-c17.md#nw-v04-c17-p0027)</sub>
- **Titles:** Teacher  <sub>[v4 c3 P32](../source/v04-c03.md#nw-v04-c03-p0032)</sub>

## Appearance

As a boy, Paul was small for his age with an delicately refined face framed in a halo of chestnut curls, crimson lips, and dark blue eyes. By sixteen, he grew to a tall six feet of manhood, with his brown curls replaced by close-cropped locks.

_Sources: [v2 c5 P7](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0007), [v2 c5 P8](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0008), [v2 c15 P11](../source/v02-c15.md#nw-v02-c15-p0011), [v3 c23 P6](../source/v03-c23.md#nw-v03-c23-p0006), [v3 c40 P2](../source/v03-c40.md#nw-v03-c40-p0002), [v4 c3 P30](../source/v04-c03.md#nw-v04-c03-p0030)_

## Personality

Paul is a sweet, sensitive, and imaginative genius with a grave and meditative side. He possesses flashes of uncanny insight and a rare, fine hidden personality that makes him easily understood by kindred spirits. Though full of dreams and fairy fancies, he is also manly, fair-minded, polite, and can hold his own among other children.

_Sources: [v2 c5 P7](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0007), [v2 c5 P8](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0008), [v2 c7 P7](../source/v02-c07.md#nw-v02-c07-p0007), [v2 c8 P52](../source/v02-c08.md#nw-v02-c08-p0052), [v2 c11 P38](../source/v02-c11.md#nw-v02-c11-p0038), [v2 c23 P36](../source/v02-c23.md#nw-v02-c23-p0036), [v2 c27 P54](../source/v02-c27.md#nw-v02-c27-p0054), [v3 c23 P6](../source/v03-c23.md#nw-v03-c23-p0006)_

## History

Paul Irving came from Boston to Avonlea to live with his grandmother, Grandma Irving, three years after his mother passed away. He attended the Avonlea school under Anne Shirley, with whom he instantly formed a bond as a kindred spirit and favorite pupil. During his schooldays, he got along well with his peers, even fighting a drawn battle with St. Clair Donnell to defend the American flag and harboring a childhood crush on Gracie Andrews. He regularly struggled with eating the generous helpings of porridge served by his grandmother, though he eventually began growing rapidly. Paul also enjoyed visits to Miss Lavendar Lewis at Echo Lodge; he later welcomed his father Stephen Irving's return and their eventual marriage, calling Miss Lavendar 'Mother Lavendar'. As he grew older, he moved to Boston with his family, traded his fairy fancies for sports like football, and developed a talent for writing poetry that earned magazine publication. He drove the carriage for Anne and Gilbert Blythe on their wedding day and wrote a lyric about a bird singing during their ceremony. Later, he made plans to go abroad for two years of study.

## Quotes

> Please, teacher, I found these in Mr. Wright’s field, and I came back to give them to you because I thought you were the kind of lady that would like them, and because . . . I like you, teacher.  <sub>[v2 c5 P21](../source/v02-c05.md#nw-v02-c05-p0021)</sub>

> I can’t do it, Grandma. I don’t really know if I can eat anything. I feel as if there was a dreadful lump in my throat. I’d have cried coming home from school if Jake Donnell hadn’t been watching me. I believe I will cry after I go to bed. It wouldn’t show on my eyes tomorrow, would it? And it would be such a relief. But anyway, I can’t eat porridge. I’m going to need all my strength of mind to bear up against this, Grandma, and I won’t have any left to grapple with porridge. Oh Grandma, I don’t know what I’ll do when my beautiful teacher goes away. Milty Boulter says he bets Jane Andrews will get the school. I suppose Miss Andrews is very nice. But I know she won’t understand things like Miss Shirley.  <sub>[v2 c26 P35](../source/v02-c26.md#nw-v02-c26-p0035)</sub>

> Oh, Miss Shirley, you can’t think what has happened! Something so splendid. Father is here . . . just think of that! Father is here! Come right in. Father, this is my beautiful teacher. You know, father.  <sub>[v2 c28 P21](../source/v02-c28.md#nw-v02-c28-p0021)</sub>

> But I don’t call her ‘mother’ just by itself. You see, that name belongs just to my own little mother, and I can’t give it to any one else. You know, teacher. But I call her ‘Mother Lavendar’ and I love her next best to father. I—I even love her a little better than you, teacher.  <sub>[v3 c23 P4](../source/v03-c23.md#nw-v03-c23-p0004)</sub>

> You’ll never grow old, Teacher. You are one of the fortunate mortals who have found and drunk from the Fountain of Youth,—you and Mother Lavendar. See here! When you’re married I WON’T call you Mrs. Blythe. To me you’ll always be 'Teacher’—the teacher of the best lessons I ever learned. I want to show you something.  <sub>[v4 c3 P32](../source/v04-c03.md#nw-v04-c03-p0032)</sub>
